title: When do machine-learning potentials need a configuration-dependent kernel? Learning long-range interactions with Fourier neural operators

paper.title: When do machine-learning potentials need a configuration-dependent kernel? Learning long-range interactions with Fourier neural operators
paper.abstract:
Abstract Long-range interactions in machine-learning interatomic potentials are commonly
treated by coupling learned sources through either a prescribed electrostatic
kernel or a learned but configuration-independent one.
Whether such a kernel suffices depends on the underlying screened interaction.
We address this question by using Fourier neural operators (FNOs) to learn
how latent source fields, built from the descriptors of a local backbone
(here MACE), interact across the simulation cell.
For a synthetic ionic system with tunable screening,
a prescribed Coulomb kernel underestimates the long-wavelength
charge fluctuations by 43 % 43\,\% under strong screening, whereas the FNO
reproduces them within 3 % 3\,\% and recovers 95 ​ – ​ 99 % 95\text{--}99\,\% of the variance of the residual left by the local backbone.
A linear FNO, which learns a configuration-independent kernel,
performs equally well in the homogeneous case.
Under inhomogeneous screening, rearranging the remote medium
modulates the coupling between distant ions,
a dependence that no configuration-independent kernel can represent.
Among the models tested, only the nonlinear FNO responds to this modulation,
and its force errors are 27 ​ – ​ 41 % 27\text{--}41\,\% lower than those of configuration-independent models.
In first-principles benchmarks of liquid water, lithium lanthanum zirconate, and Au 2 /MgO(001),
MACE– FNO \mathrm{FNO} is comparable to a prescribed-kernel model for the bulk systems
and more accurate for the interface.
It further captures the reversal of the Au 2 wetting preference
induced by remote Al dopants,
with deviations below 5 ​ meV 5\,\mathrm{meV} per cell from density functional theory.
These results indicate that a configuration-dependent kernel
becomes necessary once the screening medium varies,
even though the energy remains quadratic in the charges for a fixed medium.
Nonlinear FNOs, which learn such a kernel from energies and forces alone,
offer a flexible route to environment-dependent long-range interactions.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have made accurate atomistic simulations accessible at length and time scales beyond first-principles electronic-structure calculations. A large class of neural-network MLIPs constructs the energy from local atomic environments. In message-passing models such as MACE [ 4 ] , information is exchanged within a finite receptive field determined by the radial cutoff and the number of interaction layers. The spatial information available to each atom-centered representation is restricted to this finite receptive field. This finite range poses a strong limitation when local MLIPs are applied to systems where long-range interactions become important, such as polar liquids, ionic solids, interfaces, and adsorbate systems [ 33 , 49 , 9 ] . Their use can also be problematic when nonlocal correlation arises, e.g., through a remote charge state or collective polarization beyond the receptive field of the model. Environment-dependent atomic charges can be learned from reference charges or molecular moments and used in explicit electrostatic energies [ 50 , 47 , 21 ] . Global charge redistribution can instead be obtained through charge equilibration schemes [ 33 , 46 , 3 ] . Electronic response can also be represented through learned maximally localized Wannier centers, as in DPLR [ 53 ] , or through a self-consistently updated long-range field, as in SCFNN [ 18 ] . Approaches that do not assign explicit atomic charges include long-distance equivariant descriptors [ 24 , 27 ] , Ewald-based long-range message passing [ 34 , 44 ] , density-based long-range descriptors [ 15 ] , and attention-based global relay nodes [ 7 ] . A recent long-range-aware MLIP family learns environment-dependent sources from local descriptors and propagates them through a prescribed electrostatic kernel. Within this family, latent Ewald summation (LES) maps local invariant features to latent charge-like variables and evaluates their global coupling through a prescribed Coulomb or Ewald kernel [ 9 ] . The framework has been used to augment several local MLIPs and to recover polarization-related response from energy–force training [ 31 , 29 , 54 ] . Its source–kernel factorization is compact and interpretable when the missing interaction is well described as electrostatics. Park et al. extend this framework to latent atomic dipoles and quadrupoles, and induced charges and dipoles describe nonlocal charge redistribution and polarization through a non-self-consistent linear-response treatment [ 40 ] . The qNEP framework applies the same broad source–kernel principle within the neuroevolution potential (NEP) formalism [ 17 ] . It predicts environment-dependent atomic charges and couples them through Ewald summation or particle–particle particle–mesh electrostatics [ 16 ] . LES and qNEP demonstrate that local chemical descriptors can supply the sources of an explicit long-range operator. While a prescribed electrostatic kernel provides a strong physical prior, it confines global propagation to a chosen functional form. In a first-principles description, the bare interaction is Coulombic, and environment-dependent charges can partly represent the screening that emerges from electronic polarization [ 23 ] . The effective interaction between learned sources, however, need not take the Coulomb form between point charges. This is the case, e.g., for metallic Thomas–Fermi screening, charge transfer at interfaces, and implicit-solvent models. Learned propagation kernels offer an alternative. The reciprocal-space neural network (RSNN) couples latent atomic charge features through an isotropic reciprocal-space kernel represented by a fully connected network, which describes mixed Coulomb and Lennard-Jones interactions within a single learned form [ 25 ] . SOG-Net combines latent sources with Fourier-space kernels represented by sums of Gaussians for which the amplitudes and widths are learned to incorporate the long-range effects [ 28 ] . The long-range energy in both approaches is quadratic in the latent sources. A learned Fourier-space kernel also underlies Neural P 3 M, which uses nonlinear Fourier neural operator (FNO) blocks to account for global interactions [ 51 ] . Table 1 summarizes these approaches and how they propagate the local sources through global operators. Building on the principle of learned global propagation, here we formulate a nonlocal energy correction to a complete local backbone using the FNO [ 37 , 35 ] to propagate latent source fields derived from local atomic descriptors through spectral mixing and pointwise transformations. Unlike Neural P 3 M, the propagated fields do not feed back into the atomic message-passing layers, and the learned FNO supplies an additive correction to the local backbone. Compared with SOG-Net, which propagates each source channel independently through a sum of Gaussians, the FNO mixes the source channels at each wavevector and learns its spectral coupling for every wavelength without an assumed radial form. Stacked Fourier layers with pointwise nonlinearities further give rise to an energy that is nonquadratic in the sources, so that the effective propagation between the sources of two atoms is configuration dependent. For slabs, the operator couples sources at different heights without imposing periodicity along the surface normal. We first construct a synthetic ionic system with a Yukawa interaction to establish what the FNO learns from the residual interactions missed by the local backbone. We then introduce spatially inhomogeneous screening to assess the role of configuration-dependent propagation when the effective interaction depends on the surrounding medium. Finally, we evaluate energy and force accuracy for liquid water, Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (LLZO), and an Au 2 dimer on MgO(001). The latter also tests whether the learned correction captures the effect of remote dopants on the wetting preference of the adsorbate. Our results show that a linear FNO with a single configuration-independent propagation kernel already suffices to describe nonlocal interactions under homogeneous screening, without prior knowledge of their functional form. The nonlinear FNO, the effective propagation of which can adapt to the configuration, remains accurate for screening lengths between 2 2 and 20 ​ Å 20\,\text{\AA} and from weakly to strongly inhomogeneous screening.

sections.text: Although 𝒢 ω \mathcal{G}_{\omega} is not tied to a prescribed kernel, the learned response can still be characterized by the changes in the FNO energy upon Fourier perturbations to the latent source fields. The probe has a zero mesh integral and is normalized to an RMS amplitude of one, preserving the zero mesh integral of the source fields. sections.heading: III Homogeneous screening beyond a prescribed kernel
sections.text: Drawing on the homogeneous continuum description of screening in many bulk materials, we first construct a synthetic ionic system with spatially uniform screening. The system comprises disordered, charge-neutral NaCl-like configurations interacting through a short-range Lennard–Jones (LJ) potential and a Gaussian-smeared Yukawa potential with a tunable inverse screening length κ \kappa . Screening is made homogeneous by construction since κ \kappa is spatially constant and independent of the ionic configuration. It approaches the accuracy of the jointly trained FNO models at κ = 0.05 ​ Å − 1 \kappa=0.05\,\text{\AA}^{-1} , and becomes less reliable as the reference interaction departs further from the unscreened Coulomb form. The fact that all the FNO models maintain high accuracy across varying screening strengths clearly supports the flexibility of FNO augmentation in learning the propagation kernel. In line with the residual recovery analysis and spectral diagnostics, we find that a linear FNO suffices for the present system, and introducing nonlinearity into the field operator provides no systematic improvement in energy–force accuracy.

The interionic response is the 3 × 3 3\times 3 interatomic force-constant matrix 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} , the elements of which are K A ​ B α ​ β \displaystyle K_{AB}^{\alpha\beta} = ∂ 2 E ∂ R A ​ α ​ ∂ R B ​ β = − ∂ F A ​ α ∂ R B ​ β \displaystyle=\frac{\partial^{2}E}{\partial R_{A\alpha}\partial R_{B\beta}}=-\frac{\partial F_{A\alpha}}{\partial R_{B\beta}} (28) ≃ − F A ​ α ​ ( 𝐑 B + δ ​ 𝐞 β ) − F A ​ α ​ ( 𝐑 B − δ ​ 𝐞 β ) 2 ​ δ , \displaystyle\simeq-\frac{F_{A\alpha}(\mathbf{R}_{B}+\delta\mathbf{e}_{\beta})-F_{A\alpha}(\mathbf{R}_{B}-\delta\mathbf{e}_{\beta})}{2\delta}, where R A ​ α R_{A\alpha} and F A ​ α F_{A\alpha} are the position and force components of ion A A , α , β ∈ { x , y , z } \alpha,\beta\in\{x,y,z\} , and 𝐞 β \mathbf{e}_{\beta} is a Cartesian unit vector. We use δ = 0.05 ​ Å \delta=0.05\,\text{\AA} for the displacement of B B in the central finite differences. From one configuration of each of the 20 20 test trajectories, we select two ion pairs with minimum-image separations between 10 10 and 12 ​ Å 12\,\text{\AA} . We freeze all species within 10 ​ Å 10\,\text{\AA} of either ion of the probed pair. Outside these regions, we resample the species by Metropolis swaps at 2 800 ​ K 2\,800\,\mathrm{K} using the potential of the MD for over 1 600 1\,600 sweeps. Since the LJ interaction is invariant under the swaps, the acceptance depends only on the homogeneous Yukawa interaction among the ions and the external potential acting on S S . For each probe set, we generate five remote environments in this way: four of them are biased by an independently drawn field V ext V_{\mathrm{ext}} with V 0 = 4 V_{0}=4 (cf. Eq. ( 27 )) towards segregation of S S into different long-wavelength patterns away from the probed ions, whereas the fifth is unbiased, in favor of a uniform S S distribution. Together with the base configuration, each probe set thus provides six remote environments that differ only beyond 10 ​ Å 10\,\text{\AA} from the probed ions. The swaps preserve the composition and charge neutrality. The resampled configurations are representative of the test set, and their reference energies relative to those of the base configurations are within the standard deviation of 8.4 ​ meV ​ atom − 1 8.4\,\mathrm{meV}\,\mathrm{atom}^{-1} along the corresponding trajectories. We measure the medium-induced response by Δ ​ 𝐊 A ​ B \Delta\mathbf{K}_{AB} , the deviation of 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} from its mean over the six environments within a probe set Δ ​ 𝐊 A ​ B X , ( v ) = 𝐊 A ​ B X , ( v ) − ⟨ 𝐊 A ​ B X , ( v ′ ) ⟩ v ′ ∈ 𝒱 , \Delta\mathbf{K}_{AB}^{X,(v)}=\mathbf{K}_{AB}^{X,(v)}-\left\langle\mathbf{K}_{AB}^{X,(v^{\prime})}\right\rangle_{v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}, (29) where v v labels the six remote environments in 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , and X X refers to either an MLIP model ( X = model X=\mathrm{model} ) or the numerical reference ( X = ref X=\mathrm{ref} ). Note that pooling Δ ​ 𝐊 A ​ B \Delta\mathbf{K}_{AB} over a probe set is equivalent to comparing all 15 15 pairwise differences of 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} between its six environments. In the reference, the rearrangements of the remote medium change 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} by 0.11 ​ meV ​ Å − 2 0.11\,\mathrm{meV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2} (RMS of Δ ​ 𝐊 A ​ B \Delta\mathbf{K}_{AB} ), about 8 % 8\,\% of 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} itself (RMS of 1.42 ​ meV ​ Å − 2 1.42\,\mathrm{meV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2} ). This remote modulation stems entirely from the screened interaction as the LJ interaction between the probed ions is the same in all environments. As a null control, we generate two additional configurations per probe set in which only remote ions are exchanged at a fixed medium distribution. Here the screened Poisson equation depends only on the medium and remains fixed during ionic displacements. The quadratic screened energy thus gives a contribution to 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} that shows no dependence on the remote charges. Indeed, the reference shows no response to this null control, and any change of the model 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} would be a spurious response to the remote charges. We compare Δ ​ 𝐊 A ​ B model \Delta\mathbf{K}_{AB}^{\mathrm{model}} with Δ ​ 𝐊 A ​ B ref \Delta\mathbf{K}_{AB}^{\mathrm{ref}} in Fig. 6 , pooling all matrix elements of the six environments in the 40 40 probe sets. For each model, we report the slope b b of a linear fit as a measure of how strongly a model follows the reference modulation. Only the nonlinear MACE– FNO \mathrm{FNO} attains a slope close to unity (cf. Fig. 6 (g,h)). The local models and all the other long-range variants considered here show no appreciable response, albeit for different reasons. With a receptive field cutoff r cut = 4.5 ​ Å r_{\mathrm{cut}}=4.5\,\text{\AA} in MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} , the matrix elements of 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} are effectively zero since no atomic energy can depend on both ions when they are by construction more than 2 ​ r cut 2r_{\mathrm{cut}} apart. The deeper local MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} couples atoms with 4 ​ r cut = 18 ​ Å 4r_{\mathrm{cut}}=18\,\text{\AA} , and thus yields a nonzero 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} for the probed pairs with an RMS of 1.13 ​ meV ​ Å − 2 1.13\,\mathrm{meV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2} . The small slope b = 0.016 b=$0.016$ nevertheless shows that MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} is unable to capture the reference modulation. Indeed, a response to the remote medium requires atomic-energy contributions centered on other atoms to depend jointly on the probed pair and the rearranged medium. This is a more restrictive requirement than coupling the two ions alone, and the maximum coupling range of 18 ​ Å 18\,\text{\AA} does not ensure that shared local environments capture the medium dependence of this coupling. MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} – LES \mathrm{LES} , CACE–SOG, and the linear MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} – FNO \mathrm{FNO} couple the probed ions through a long-range kernel, as manifested by the 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} RMS of 1.4 ​ – ​ 1.6 ​ meV ​ Å − 2 1.4\text{--}1.6\,\mathrm{meV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2} , comparable to that of the reference. Although S S atoms contribute to the latent source field, the independence of these kernels from the screening medium prevents remote S S rearrangements from modifying the propagation operator coupling the probed ions. Hence, these fixed-kernel models capture an effective interionic coupling but miss its modulation by the remote screening medium, leaving 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} constant across the six environments. In the linear FNO, remote S S sources only add to the field. In the nonlinear FNO, they also modify the effective propagation between the probed ions, so 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} responds to the remote-medium rearrangements. With joint training, the nonlinear FNO attains a seed-averaged slope of b = 1.13 ± 0.02 b=$1.13$\pm$0.02$ , and the slope within each probe set is positive in all 40 40 sets for every seed. A comparable slope is obtained with the frozen MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} backbone ( b = 1.09 ± 0.06 b=$1.09$\pm$0.06$ ). We further quantify the element-wise agreement by the coefficient of determination of the predictions, R 2 = 1 − ∑ ( Δ ​ K model − Δ ​ K ref ) 2 / ∑ ( Δ ​ K ref ) 2 R^{2}=1-\sum(\Delta K^{\mathrm{model}}-\Delta K^{\mathrm{ref}})^{2}/\sum(\Delta K^{\mathrm{ref}})^{2} , which vanishes for a model without response and reaches unity only when every matrix element is reproduced. The joint nonlinear FNO achieves R 2 = 0.60 ± 0.02 R^{2}=$0.60$\pm$0.02$ , higher than that of the frozen one ( R 2 = 0.42 ± 0.08 R^{2}=$0.42$\pm$0.08$ ). The scatter in MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} – FNO \mathrm{FNO} is in part a spurious response to remote ionic charges at a fixed distribution of the screening medium. In the null control, the nonlinear FNO changes 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} by an RMS of 0.03 ​ – ​ 0.05 ​ meV ​ Å − 2 0.03\text{--}0.05\,\mathrm{meV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2} , about half that of the scatter. This spurious sensitivity presumably arises because the sources of remote ions can modify the effective propagation in the nonlinear FNO as those of S S do, and the architecture does not enforce the invariance of the reference to remote ionic rearrangement. For 𝐊 A ​ B \mathbf{K}_{AB} itself, the joint nonlinear FNO gives the lowest RMSE ( 0.29 ​ meV ​ Å − 2 0.29\,\mathrm{meV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2} , compared with 0.41 0.41 for the joint linear FNO, 0.43 0.43 for CACE–SOG, and 0.64 ​ meV ​ Å − 2 0.64\,\mathrm{meV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2} for LES). Note that none of the models is trained on force constants, and the probe provides an independent test of the learned coupling. It supports the interpretation of the force errors in Sec. IV.1 : among the models studied here, only the nonlinear FNO captures a substantial part of the reference modulation of the interionic coupling by the remote screening medium.

sections.heading: V First-principles benchmarks
sections.text: Alongside the synthetic benchmark, we consider liquid water, lithium lanthanum zirconate (LLZO), and Au 2 /MgO(001) with remote Al dopants. These benchmarks are collected from existing datasets using first-principles references. Liquid water represents a prototypical system in which local hydrogen bonding combines with long-range electrostatic coupling between polar water molecules [ 18 ] . This coupling influences collective polarization and dielectric screening, which can be misrepresented by short-range MLIPs [ 9 ] . We examine whether our MACE– FNO \mathrm{FNO} can improve energy and force predictions beyond a compact local MACE description. The liquid-water dataset released with the qNEP study [ 16 ] contains reference energies and forces calculated at the meta-GGA SCAN level [ 48 ] . The structures contain 128 128 water molecules ( 384 384 atoms) in an aligned cubic cell. Removing exact duplicate geometries from the released 1 388 1\,388 -entry training pool results in 523 523 distinct configurations to be used in this study. A cell-length-stratified split with seed 17 17 assigns 471 471 to training and 52 52 to validation. From the released 500 500 -entry validation file, we select the 134 134 unique geometries absent from the source training pool as our test set. All local MACE, MACE– FNO \mathrm{FNO} , and MACE– LES \mathrm{LES} models share this geometry-disjoint split. LLZO is a garnet-type solid electrolyte with mobile lithium ions in an oxide framework. In LLZO, lithium ions interact electrostatically with other lithium ions and the extended La-Zr-O network, giving rise to long-range interactions that go beyond their immediate coordination shell. For LLZO, we take the 1 978 1\,978 reference structures originally generated by Yan and Zhu [ 52 ] and redistributed by Fan et al. with the qNEP study [ 16 ] . The reference calculations employ the PBEsol functional [ 43 ] . The structures contain 192 192 atoms per periodic cell. The unit cell sizes and shapes vary across the dataset. As the release provides no predefined training and test partition, we assign consecutive source blocks of 20 20 structures using seed 17 17 , obtaining 1 578 1\,578 training, 200 200 validation, and 200 200 test structures. Since the release does not identify the trajectories from which the structures are drawn, test blocks may share a trajectory with training blocks. The local baselines, frozen and joint MACE– FNO \mathrm{FNO} , and MACE– LES \mathrm{LES} models share this data partition. The Au 2 dimer adsorbed on MgO(001) extends our benchmarks from bulk systems to a two-dimensional surface system. Depending on its axis orientation relative to the MgO surface, the dimer can adopt either a wetting (parallel) or a non-wetting (upright) configuration. Theoretical studies have shown that electron-donor doping can stabilize flat Au clusters on MgO through charge transfer [ 38 , 39 ] . Interestingly, the geometry preference of the dimer can be modified by subsurface Al dopants located more than 10 ​ Å 10\,\text{\AA} away [ 33 ] . Such a long-range correlation provides a direct test of sensitivity to remote chemical changes. We use 5 000 5\,000 configurations with DFT energies and forces generated by Ko et al. [ 33 ] using the PBE functional [ 42 ] . We adopt the split of 4 500 4\,500 training and 500 500 test structures released with the LES study of Kim et al. [ 29 ] . For FNO and LES training, we reserve 225 225 training structures for internal validation, leaving 4 275 4\,275 for fitting. For liquid water and LLZO, we train the local MACE baselines from scratch with a 4.5 ​ Å 4.5\,\text{\AA} cutoff and 128 128 scalar hidden features. For Au 2 /MgO(001), we adopt the one-interaction local MACE checkpoint released with the LES study [ 29 ] and train a two-interaction baseline. Both use a 5.5 ​ Å 5.5\,\text{\AA} cutoff and 128 128 scalar and 128 128 vector channels per interaction. In addition to the one-interaction backbone, we augment the two-interaction backbone with FNO and LES to assess whether global corrections provide further accuracy gains beyond those achieved by extending the local receptive field. The two-interaction FNO extension follows the same fitting protocol as the one-interaction runs, including the loss scales, learning-rate schedule, and checkpoint-selection rule. The two-interaction source head receives 256 256 invariant descriptors from the two interactions instead of 128 128 . The source-head hidden width and all FNO settings are unchanged. We adopt the FNO settings in Table 2 . For all three systems, we use a hidden-channel width H f = 16 H_{f}=$16$ for the Fourier layers and mix all hidden channels through a single spectral channel group ( G = 1 G=1 ). For Au 2 /MgO(001), we report the results obtained with full z z -mixing over 24 24 height points within the spectral matrix [Eq. ( 5 )]. The channel-wise mixing results are presented in Appendix B.3 . To reduce spurious energy and force changes under rigid translation relative to the mesh, we average the FNO energy corrections over four in-plane mesh origins for Au 2 /MgO(001). These correspond to all combinations of zero and half-grid shifts along the two periodic directions. This interlacing is applied during both training and inference. Liquid water and LLZO are evaluated on a single mesh, since interlacing changes their energy and force RMSEs only marginally (Appendix B.1 ). sections.heading: V.1 Energy and force accuracy
sections.text: As summarized in Table 6 , FNO augmentation substantially improves the accuracy of the one-interaction backbone for liquid water, LLZO, and Au 2 /MgO(001). With the frozen MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} backbone, nonlinear FNO already reduces the energy RMSE by 40 ​ – ​ 51 % 40\text{--}51\,\% and the force RMSE by 23 ​ – ​ 43 % 23\text{--}43\,\% for the two bulk systems. The gains are particularly sizable for Au 2 /MgO(001), reaching 97 % 97\,\% for energy and 90 % 90\,\% for forces. Training the backbone and FNO jointly further lowers the force RMSE by 9 ​ – ​ 37 % 9\text{--}37\,\% in all three systems and the energy RMSE by 10 % ​ and ​ 37 % 10\,\%\text{ and }37\,\% for water and LLZO, respectively. Most of the improvement over the local baseline is, however, already obtained with linear FNO. With joint training, MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} – FNO ( l ) \mathrm{FNO}^{(\mathrm{l})} accounts for 86 ​ – ​ 100 % 86\text{--}100\,\% of the RMSE reduction achieved by MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} – FNO \mathrm{FNO} . Nonlinearity mainly benefits the forces of LLZO and Au 2 /MgO(001), whose RMSEs decrease by a further 18 % ​ and ​ 23 % 18\,\%\text{ and }23\,\% , respectively, while both RMSEs of water change by only 3 % 3\,\% . Increasing the depth of the local backbone largely reduces the errors of MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} , lowering the energy RMSE by 75 ​ – ​ 93 % 75\text{--}93\,\% and the force RMSE by 66 ​ – ​ 94 % 66\text{--}94\,\% . MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} is also more accurate than all MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} – FNO \mathrm{FNO} models except for the energy of Au 2 /MgO(001), for which the FNO models give lower RMSEs. Adding FNO to this deeper MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} backbone further improves the accuracy, although the gains become smaller, particularly for the forces. The jointly trained MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} – FNO \mathrm{FNO} lowers the energy RMSE by 24 % ​ , ​ 6 % ​ , and ​ 56 % 24\,\%\text{, }6\,\%\text{, and }56\,\% and the force RMSE by 2 % ​ , ​ 10 % ​ , and ​ 12 % 2\,\%\text{, }10\,\%\text{, and }12\,\% for water, LLZO, and Au 2 /MgO(001), respectively. It is clear that joint training becomes less important as the receptive field of the backbone extends. Whereas joint training reduces the energy and force RMSEs of MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} – FNO \mathrm{FNO} by up to 37 % 37\,\% , it changes the RMSEs of MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} – FNO \mathrm{FNO} by less than 4 % 4\,\% . Nonlinearity likewise loses its advantage with the deeper backbone, as the force RMSEs of the linear and nonlinear FNO differ by less than 4 % 4\,\% for all three systems. The gains from nonlinearity with MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} in LLZO and Au 2 /MgO(001) thus point to the limited one-interaction backbone rather than to configuration-dependent screening. The pretrained MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} representation, in turn, already supplies most of what the FNO correction requires. We now compare FNO with LES on the same local backbones. The accuracies of the two approaches are comparable for the two bulk systems. With MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} , FNO gives a lower energy RMSE for water and agrees with LES within the seed spread for LLZO, while LES gives a slightly lower force RMSE for water. With MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} , FNO retains the lower energy RMSE for water, and the force RMSEs are lower with LES for both systems. The learned propagation thus reaches an accuracy comparable to that of the prescribed Coulomb kernel in LES for the two bulk systems, where learned charges can partly represent the polarization. sections.heading: V.2 Remote-dopant wetting preference
sections.text: Remote Al dopants in the MgO(001) substrate present a stringent test for nonlocal MLIPs. We define the wetting preference for the adsorbed Au 2 dimer as the relative energy of the wetting (parallel) and non-wetting (upright) configurations Δ ​ E wet = E ⁡ ( wetting ) − E ⁡ ( non ​ - ​ wetting ) . \Delta E_{\mathrm{wet}}=E(\mathrm{wetting})-E(\mathrm{non\mbox{-}wetting}). (30) On undoped MgO, a non-wetting dimer configuration is favored according to the PBE calculations [ 33 ] . Al dopants in the substrate lead to a sign reversal in Δ ​ E wet \Delta E_{\mathrm{wet}} , thereby indicating a stabilized wetting configuration. This reversal cannot be described by local MACE models with a receptive field too short to couple the dimer to the dopants [ 31 , 29 ] . With a cutoff of 5.5 ​ Å 5.5\,\text{\AA} , the one-interaction MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} couples only atoms within 11 ​ Å 11\,\text{\AA} of each other, whereas the nearest dimer–dopant separation is 11.1 ​ – ​ 11.4 ​ Å 11.1\text{--}11.4\,\text{\AA} in the non-wetting and wetting geometries. The second interaction layer of MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} extends this coupling range to 22 ​ Å 22\,\text{\AA} . The reach of the local backbones is directly manifested in the wetting preferences shown in Table 7 . While MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} predicts essentially the same Δ ​ E wet \Delta E_{\mathrm{wet}} on both substrates, MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} reproduces the sign reversal upon Al doping. The sign reversal is also reproduced when augmenting MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} with FNO or LES. The nonlinear MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} – FNO \mathrm{FNO} predicts wetting preferences within 5 ​ meV 5\,\mathrm{meV} per cell of the DFT values on both substrates, with seed spreads below 1 ​ meV 1\,\mathrm{meV} . For comparison, MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} – LES \mathrm{LES} and MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} deviate by up to 10 ​ meV ​ and ​ 32 ​ meV 10\,\mathrm{meV}\text{ and }32\,\mathrm{meV} , respectively. Linear FNO is at least as accurate on doped MgO but deviates by up to 9 ​ meV 9\,\mathrm{meV} on undoped MgO. Finally, with the deeper MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} backbone, FNO augmentation reduces the deviations further to below 4 ​ meV 4\,\mathrm{meV} , while MACE 2 \mathrm{MACE}_{2} – LES \mathrm{LES} still deviates by up to 20 ​ meV 20\,\mathrm{meV} . Table 7 shows that all MLIPs except MACE 1 \mathrm{MACE}_{1} place both endpoints below the reference DFT-PBE energies. For the FNO models, these offsets amount to 44 ​ – ​ 53 ​ meV 44\text{--}53\,\mathrm{meV} on undoped and 27 ​ – ​ 31 ​ meV 27\text{--}31\,\mathrm{meV} on Al-doped MgO, equivalent to 0.25 ​ – ​ 0.48 ​ meV ​ atom − 1 0.25\text{--}0.48\,\mathrm{meV}\,\mathrm{atom}^{-1} , about three to seven times the test energy RMSE. The offsets are already present at the DFT geometries, as relaxation changes the endpoint energies of these models by less than 0.2 ​ meV 0.2\,\mathrm{meV} . We note that the dataset consists of 1 250 1\,250 perturbed configurations around each of the four endpoints but not the relaxed endpoints themselves. The offsets therefore indicate a common error in extrapolating to the basin minima. With the FNO models, the offsets are found to be more consistent between the wetting and non-wetting configurations, thereby largely canceling in Δ ​ E wet \Delta E_{\mathrm{wet}} .

sections.heading: VII Conclusions and outlook
sections.text: We have introduced FNO augmentation as a distinct route to nonlocal MLIPs by learning the global coupling between latent source fields. Added as a nonlocal correction term to a complete local backbone, the learned operator captures long-range interactions accurately beyond the local receptive field, and, where a reference kernel is known, the learned response can be compared directly with it through spectral analysis in reciprocal space. A central strength of our framework is its flexibility in describing long-range interactions without adhering to a specific kernel. A prescribed Coulomb kernel is a useful prior when the residual interaction is largely electrostatic, but its predictive power becomes limited once the effective interaction between the sources departs from the Coulomb form, e.g., through screening set by the environment. The learned operator overcomes this limitation by adapting its wavevector dependence to the interaction at hand. On a synthetic ionic system with tunable screened Coulomb interactions, the FNO recovers 95 ​ – ​ 99 % 95\text{--}99\,\% of the variance of the residual left by the local MACE backbone and, with joint training, consistently outperforms a prescribed-kernel long-range model and a deeper local model at all three screening lengths tested. It further reproduces the long-wavelength charge–charge structure factor of the ionic fluid in both the nearly Coulombic and the strongly screened regimes. Note that low energy and force errors do not by themselves guarantee correct long-wavelength charge fluctuations, which underlie dielectric response and ion solvation. Reproducing these correlations in its own sampled ensemble without explicitly including the structure factor in the training indicates that the learned operator reproduces the collective consequences of the residual interaction, not only the training labels. With inhomogeneous screening, the interaction can no longer be described by a configuration-independent propagation kernel. Among the models considered here, only the nonlinear FNO captures the modulation of the coupling between distant ions by the remote screening medium, which LES, CACE–SOG, and the linear FNO leave unchanged. Its force RMSE is also 27 ​ – ​ 41 % 27\text{--}41\,\% lower than those of these models. We expect learned operators of this kind to be particularly useful where the effective interaction between learned sources departs from the Coulomb form or varies with the surrounding configuration. Among the first-principles benchmarks, Au 2 /MgO(001) provides an example, in which remote dopants beyond the reach of the local backbone reverse the wetting preference of the adsorbed dimer through charge transfer [ 38 , 39 ] . The FNO captures this reversal more accurately than both LES and a deeper local backbone. For liquid water and LLZO, FNO augmentation also substantially lowers the errors of the one-interaction backbone, but reaches an accuracy comparable to that of LES, consistent with environment-dependent charges partly representing the screening from electronic polarization [ 23 ] . Note that these first-principles benchmarks are restricted to static energies and forces. Beyond the present benchmarks, learned operators could thus be relevant to electrolytes and solvated interfaces near electrodes, doped and defective oxides and semiconductors, and metal–insulator interfaces where charge transfer and image charges reshape the long-range response. Finally, connecting the learned response to a physically defined polarization could enable predictions of Born effective charges through its derivatives with respect to atomic positions [ 22 ] . The present MACE– FNO \mathrm{FNO} implementation does not identify physical charge densities in the latent fields. An extension would require a consistent polarization definition and additional physical constraints or response supervision. These observables could both constrain the learned operator and test its description of nonlocal polarization response. Acknowledgements. sections.heading: A.4.1 Metric-aware EqGINO for bulk and slabs
sections.text: An unconstrained FNO learns independent channel-mixing matrices for different wavevectors, so that rotating a field need not rotate the predicted response. Following EqGINO [ 30 ] , we impose isotropic weight sharing, in which modes of the same wavelength share a matrix, R ℓ ​ ( 𝐤 ) = 𝖱 ℓ ​ ( | 𝐤 | 2 ) R_{\ell}(\mathbf{k})=\mathsf{R}_{\ell}(|\mathbf{k}|^{2}) , with | 𝐤 | |\mathbf{k}| the in-plane wavevector magnitude for slabs. Here we adopt this spectral principle in place of the full EqGINO encoder–decoder architecture. The response transforms with the input field under rotations and reflections that preserve the cell, mesh, and selected mode band. For slabs, this statement applies to in-plane transformations. This construction does not guarantee equivariance under arbitrary rotations on a fixed mesh or invariance under arbitrary changes of lattice basis. Isotropy constrains the spectral matrices. The linearized response of the nonlinear operator about a given atomic configuration can nevertheless be anisotropic, as the spatial arrangement of the sources can break rotational symmetry. Since the same integer Fourier index represents different wavelengths in cells of different sizes or shapes, we evaluate the learned matrices at physical wavevector magnitudes. Their values are learned at the reciprocal-space shells of a fixed cubic or square reference cell and interpolated by a natural cubic spline in | 𝐤 | 2 |\mathbf{k}|^{2} , which reduces to independent shell weights at the reference cell. Outside the knot interval, we extrapolate linearly along the endpoint tangents. All systems in this work use one spectral channel group ( G = 1 G=1 ). In the nonlinear FNO, the local matrix W ℓ W_{\ell} also mixes all channels. For liquid water, the cell features 𝐪 𝐇 \mathbf{q}_{\mathbf{H}} supply ln ⁡ L \ln L with L = | det 𝐇 | 1 / 3 L=|\det\mathbf{H}|^{1/3} in Å \mathrm{\text{\AA}} , and LLZO additionally receives the six independent components of 𝐇𝐇 𝖳 / L 2 \mathbf{H}\mathbf{H}^{\mathsf{T}}/L^{2} to describe the cell shape. With the lattice vectors stored as rows of 𝐇 \mathbf{H} , these features are constant across the mesh and invariant under rigid rotation of the whole cell. The fixed-cell slab has no cell features.

Learning long-range interactions with Fourier neural operators Wei Chen Email: wei.chen@uclouvain.be Affiliation: Institute of Condensed Matter and Nanosciences (IMCN), UCLouvain, Louvain-la-Neuve, Belgium Gian-Marco Rignanese Email: gian-marco.rignanese@uclouvain.be Affiliation: Institute of Condensed Matter and Nanosciences (IMCN), UCLouvain, Louvain-la-Neuve, Belgium Affiliation: WEL Research Institute, Wavre, Belgium October 21, 2026 Abstract Long-range interactions in machine-learning interatomic potentials are commonly treated by coupling learned sources through either a prescribed electrostatic kernel or a learned but configuration-independent one. Whether such a kernel suffices depends on the underlying screened interaction. We address this question by using Fourier neural operators (FNOs) to learn how latent source fields, built from the descriptors of a local backbone (here MACE), interact across the simulation cell. For a synthetic ionic system with tunable screening, a prescribed Coulomb kernel underestimates the long-wavelength charge fluctuations by 43 % 43\,\% under strong screening, whereas the FNO reproduces them within 3 % 3\,\% and recovers 95 ​ – ​ 99 % 95\text{--}99\,\% of the variance of the residual left by the local backbone. A linear FNO, which learns a configuration-independent kernel, performs equally well in the homogeneous case. Under inhomogeneous screening, rearranging the remote medium modulates the coupling between distant ions, a dependence that no configuration-independent kernel can represent. Among the models tested, only the nonlinear FNO responds to this modulation, and its force errors are 27 ​ – ​ 41 % 27\text{--}41\,\% lower than those of configuration-independent models. In first-principles benchmarks of liquid water, lithium lanthanum zirconate, and Au 2 /MgO(001), MACE– FNO \mathrm{FNO} is comparable to a prescribed-kernel model for the bulk systems and more accurate for the interface. It further captures the reversal of the Au 2 wetting preference induced by remote Al dopants, with deviations below 5 ​ meV 5\,\mathrm{meV} per cell from density functional theory. These results indicate that a configuration-dependent kernel becomes necessary once the screening medium varies, even though the energy remains quadratic in the charges for a fixed medium. Nonlinear FNOs, which learn such a kernel from energies and forces alone, offer a flexible route to environment-dependent long-range interactions. I Introduction Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have made accurate atomistic simulations accessible at length and time scales beyond first-principles electronic-structure calculations. A large class of neural-network MLIPs constructs the energy from local atomic environments. In message-passing models such as MACE [ 4 ] , information is exchanged within a finite receptive field determined by the radial cutoff and the number of interaction layers. The spatial information available to each atom-centered representation is restricted to this finite receptive field. This finite range poses a strong limitation when local MLIPs are applied to systems where long-range interactions become important, such as polar liquids, ionic solids, interfaces, and adsorbate systems [ 33 , 49 , 9 ] . Their use can also be problematic when nonlocal correlation arises, e.g., through a remote charge state or collective polarization beyond the receptive field of the model. Environment-dependent atomic charges can be learned from reference charges or molecular moments and used in explicit electrostatic energies [ 50 , 47 , 21 ] . Global charge redistribution can instead be obtained through charge equilibration schemes [ 33 , 46 , 3 ] . Electronic response can also be represented through learned maximally localized Wannier centers, as in DPLR [ 53 ] , or through a self-consistently updated long-range field, as in SCFNN [ 18 ] . Approaches that do not assign explicit atomic charges include long-distance equivariant descriptors [ 24 , 27 ] , Ewald-based long-range message passing [ 34 , 44 ] , density-based long-range descriptors [ 15 ] , and attention-based global relay nodes [ 7 ] . A recent long-range-aware MLIP family learns environment-dependent sources from local descriptors and propagates them through a prescribed electrostatic kernel. Within this family, latent Ewald summation (LES) maps local invariant features to latent charge-like variables and evaluates their global coupling through a prescribed Coulomb or Ewald kernel [ 9 ] . The framework has been used to augment several local MLIPs and to recover polarization-related response from energy–force training [ 31 , 29 , 54 ] . Its source–kernel factorization is compact and interpretable when the missing interaction is well described as electrostatics. Park et al. extend this framework to latent atomic dipoles and quadrupoles, and induced charges and dipoles describe nonlocal charge redistribution and polarization through a non-self-consistent linear-response treatment [ 40 ] . The qNEP framework applies the same broad source–kernel principle within the neuroevolution potential (NEP) formalism [ 17 ] . It predicts environment-dependent atomic charges and couples them through Ewald summation or particle–particle particle–mesh electrostatics [ 16 ] . LES and qNEP demonstrate that local chemical descriptors can supply the sources of an explicit long-range operator. While a prescribed electrostatic kernel provides a strong physical prior, it confines global propagation to a chosen functional form. In a first-principles description, the bare interaction is Coulombic, and environment-dependent charges can partly represent the screening that emerges from electronic polarization [ 23 ] . The effective interaction between learned sources, however, need not take the Coulomb form between point charges. This is the case, e.g., for metallic Thomas–Fermi screening, charge transfer at interfaces, and implicit-solvent models. Learned propagation kernels offer an alternative. The reciprocal-space neural network (RSNN) couples latent atomic charge features through an isotropic reciprocal-space kernel represented by a fully connected network, which describes mixed Coulomb and Lennard-Jones interactions within a single learned form [ 25 ] . SOG-Net combines latent sources with Fourier-space kernels represented by sums of Gaussians for which the amplitudes and widths are learned to incorporate the long-range effects [ 28 ] . The long-range energy in both approaches is quadratic in the latent sources. A learned Fourier-space kernel also underlies Neural P 3 M, which uses nonlinear Fourier neural operator (FNO) blocks to account for global interactions [ 51 ] . Table 1 summarizes these approaches and how they propagate the local sources through global operators. Building on the principle of learned global propagation, here we formulate a nonlocal energy correction to a complete local backbone using the FNO [ 37 , 35 ] to propagate latent source fields derived from local atomic descriptors through spectral mixing and pointwise transformations. Unlike Neural P 3 M, the propagated fields do not feed back into the atomic message-passing layers, and the learned FNO supplies an additive correction to the local backbone. Compared with SOG-Net, which propagates each source channel independently through a sum of Gaussians, the FNO mixes the source channels at each wavevector and learns its spectral coupling for every wavelength without an assumed radial form. Stacked Fourier layers with pointwise nonlinearities further give rise to an energy that is nonquadratic in the sources, so that the effective propagation between the sources of two atoms is configuration dependent. For slabs, the operator couples sources at different heights without imposing periodicity along the surface normal. We first construct a synthetic ionic system with a Yukawa interaction to establish what the FNO learns from the residual interactions missed by the local backbone. We then introduce spatially inhomogeneous screening to assess the role of configuration-dependent propagation when the effective interaction depends on the surrounding medium. Finally, we evaluate energy and force accuracy for liquid water, Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (LLZO), and an Au 2 dimer on MgO(001). The latter also tests whether the learned correction captures the effect of remote dopants on the wetting preference of the adsorbate. Our results show that a linear FNO with a single configuration-independent propagation kernel already suffices to describe nonlocal interactions under homogeneous screening, without prior knowledge of their functional form. The nonlinear FNO, the effective propagation of which can adapt to the configuration, remains accurate for screening lengths between 2 2 and 20 ​ Å 20\,\text{\AA} and from weakly to strongly inhomogeneous screening. III Homogeneous screening beyond a prescribed kernel Drawing on the homogeneous continuum description of screening in many bulk materials, we first construct a synthetic ionic system with spatially uniform screening.
